title: Why must PS be as long as PQ in the square?
description: In the square PQRS with PQ of six centimetres, the length of PS is found from the property that all sides of a square are equal, with no ruler needed. Keeko raises the doubt that every side must be measured.
teaching_notes: One idea: one known side of a square gives the length of every other side, because all sides are equal. Watch for children who think each side must be measured to know it.

source: In the construction of square PQRS with PQ = 6 cm, can you see why PS should be 6 cm long?
video_script.why: The child uses the property that all sides of a square are equal to explain the length of PS in the construction.
video_script.substitution: A square PQRS with PQ of 6 cm, drawn with a perpendicular at P.
video_script.anchor: A square PQRS under construction, with PQ of 6 cm along the bottom and the perpendicular through P standing above P
video_script.wrong_answer: we must measure every side with a ruler
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks we must measure every side with a ruler to know its length. All sides of a square are equal, so one known side gives every other side, and the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: All sides of a square are equal, so P S is six centimetres.

final_answer.value: because all sides of a square are equal, PS = PQ = 6 cm
final_answer.spoken: all sides of a square are equal, so P S is six centimetres

never_show: the length of PS before the answer
maths_rules: Property S1: all 4 sides of a square are equal.
PS and PQ are two sides of the square that meet at P.
PQ = 6 cm, so PS = PQ = 6 cm.
By the same property, QR = 6 cm and RS = 6 cm.
Folding a square paper corner to corner lays the two sides at the corner exactly on each other, so they are equal.
video_script.design: One idea: the equal-sides property gives PS from PQ. Uses the first property of a square. Wrong idea: every side must be measured. The square stays all video.
